item_taken.first_six_words: Absent owner's clock: a deadline whose
item_taken.why: The case names its own carrier as another party's calendar, Kestrel's 15 October plan lock drawn up without reference to her and brought to Ostrava's table as a deadline Ostrava could not soften, which is this item's mechanism exactly; it is not Tied hands, which borrows an absent owner's refusal rather than its date (no one at Kestrel refused anything), not Fed suitor, since Kestrel was given nothing and had no wants in play (she sent it nothing), and not Walk on record or Silent floor, since the option was claimed aloud on 20 August and rested on a document and a date, not a past exit or a private floor.

reasoning: The rule sorts by question: making an alternative exist in a counterparty's model, and its cost, stays here; how an alternative that never occurs changes the episode it shadows goes across. The case holds both, but its mass is on the far side. The making is one act, the letter of 20 August, and its keeping cost is paid in the item's own coin, letting the clock bind, which she did by sending Kestrel nothing and letting the line fold. Everything the case then records is the shadow's work on the actual episode: Ostrava conceded the level on 9 October against the return, wrote it into the draft offer, noted in its file that the level was granted against the Kestrel return, and on 20 November issued and she signed a contract at that level five weeks after the return had stopped existing. The return never occurred within the episode, and the carriers by which it changed the episode are identifiable (the conceded level, the draft offer, the offer-file note, the signed contract). The case also holds the target's second clause directly: at Kestrel the unlived return prevented any carrier or witness from forming, since no one organized a use for her desk, the two engineers taking her duties had not asked for them, no one was asked about her, and no one opposed or declined her. So the rule places the case on the target's side; what stays here is only the residue the rule names, the 20 August manufacture and the cost of letting the clock run out, and the case is not about that residue but about what the manufactured, never-taken alternative did to the offer that was signed.
case_out: Within the episode of Ines Farro's negotiation of an offer from Ostrava Labs (August to November 2026), a represented alternative, her return to Kestrel Systems under an undated letter promising an equivalent post after open-ended unpaid leave since 1 September 2025, did not occur: she never returned to Kestrel, and after 15 October 2026 the return was unexercisable, employment there afterwards being a new hire from outside. The alternative was represented to Ostrava once, in her letter of 20 August 2026: 'Kestrel's plan locks on 15 October and my post lapses with it; settle the level before then or I go back.' It changed the actual episode through identifiable carriers: the level Ostrava conceded on 9 October 2026, the draft offer into which Ostrava wrote that level, Ostrava's offer-file note that the level was 'granted against the Kestrel return', and the contract she signed on 20 November 2026 at that level, issued only after an export-control screening completed on 18 November, five weeks after the alternative it was conceded against had stopped existing. The alternative also prevented a carrier or witness from forming on Kestrel's side: she sent Kestrel nothing between 20 August and 15 October; on 15 October 2026 Kestrel's headcount plan, which locks every 15 October and was drawn up without reference to her, folded her line into two existing posts; no one at Kestrel had organized a use for her desk, the two engineers taking her duties had not asked for them, no one was asked about her, and no one opposed or declined her return.
